Student ID: IT22145976

Question 1
a) ACID properties are Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Atomicity means all or nothing, enforced by logging. Consistency means database remains valid, enforced by constraints. Isolation means transactions don't interfere, enforced by locking. Durability means committed data survives crashes, enforced by WAL.

Basic 2PL cascading rollback example:
T1: R(A), W(A)
T2: R(A), W(B)
T3: R(B), W(C)
If T1 aborts after T2 reads A, T2 must abort, and T3 must abort because it read B from T2.
Strict 2PL prevents this by holding all locks until commit.

View serializable but not conflict serializable:
T1: W(A)
T2: W(A), W(B)
T3: R(A), W(B)
This has write-write conflict on A between T1 and T2. View equivalent to T1 then T2 then T3 because T3 reads A from T2 and final write on B is from T3.

b) MVCC creates multiple versions of data. Readers don't block writers. Traditional locking blocks. Snapshot isolation means each transaction sees a snapshot. Write skew is when two transactions read same data and write different data causing constraint violation.
Example: X=50, Y=50. T1 reads X=50, Y=50, writes X=-40. T2 reads X=50, Y=50, writes Y=-40. Both commit. Now X+Y=-80 which violates X+Y>0.
SSI detects this by tracking dependencies between transactions and aborts one.

Question 2
a) ARIES has three phases: Analysis, Redo, Undo. Analysis scans log from checkpoint to build transaction table and dirty page table. Redo repeats all updates from the log. Undo undoes loser transactions. CLRs are compensation log records written during undo.

Dirty page table tracks which pages are dirty and their earliest LSN. Transaction table tracks active transactions and their last LSN.

Example operations:
T1 updates page P1, log record L1
T2 updates page P2, log record L2
T1 commits, log record L3
Crash happens
During recovery: Analysis finds T2 active. Redo applies L1 and L2. Undo undoes T2 using L2 and writes CLR.

b) UNDO logging logs before images. REDO logging logs after images. UNDO/REDO logs both. Steal policy allows writing uncommitted data to disk. Force policy writes committed data to disk immediately. UNDO logging needs no-steal. REDO logging needs no-force. UNDO/REDO supports steal and no-force.

Physiological logging logs page-level physical changes but logical within page. Example: insert tuple into page 5 at offset 20.

Question 3
a) Clustered index stores records in index order. Non-clustered index has pointers to records. Range queries faster with clustered index because sequential access. Single record lookup similar.

Employee table example: Employee(ID, Name, Dept). Non-clustered index on Dept. Index-only scan on Dept reads only index pages, maybe 3 pages. Full table scan reads 1000 pages. Clustered index on ID makes range scan on ID sequential.

b) Extendible hashing uses directory and buckets. Global depth and local depth. When bucket overflows, split bucket and maybe double directory.

Insert 1,2,3,4,5,6,7 with capacity 3:
Initially global depth 1, two buckets.
After 1,2,3: bucket 0 has 1,2,3 (overflow? No, capacity is 3)
Insert 4: bucket splits, global depth becomes 2
Continue showing evolution.

Linear hashing splits buckets linearly. Uses overflow chains. Directory grows slowly.

Average block access: Extendible 1-2 blocks, Linear 1-3 blocks.

Question 4
a) External merge sort sorts runs and merges. Hybrid hash join partitions and joins in memory. Grace hash join partitions both relations. Block nested loop join scans repeatedly.

5-pass external merge sort: cost = 2 * 5000 * 5 = 50000 I/O.
Hybrid hash join with 25% memory reserved: cost = 3 * 5000 - 2 * (0.25 * 50 * 50) = 15000 - 1250 = 13750 I/O.

b) Volcano model processes row by row with function calls. Vectorized execution processes batches. MPP uses multiple nodes. Columnar storage stores data column by column. Compression reduces I/O. JIT compilation generates machine code for specific queries.

Star schema join query benefits from JIT because join loops are compiled.

Question 1
a) ACID: Atomicity means either all operations happen or none. Consistency means database goes from one valid state to another. Isolation means transactions appear to run serially. Durability means committed data is permanent. Enforced by: Atomicity via undo logging, Consistency via constraints and triggers, Isolation via locking or MVCC, Durability via redo logging and WAL.

Basic 2PL cascading rollback:
T1: R(A), W(A)
T2: R(A), W(B)
T3: R(B), W(C)
T1 aborts after T2 reads uncommitted A. T2 must abort, causing T3 to abort because it read uncommitted B from T2. This is cascading rollback.
Strict 2PL: T1 holds all locks until it commits. So T2 cannot read A until T1 commits, preventing cascading rollback.

View serializable but not conflict serializable schedule:
T1: W(A)
T2: W(A), W(B)
T3: R(A), W(B)
Conflict graph: T1->T2 on A, T2->T3 on A? T3 reads A from T2 so T2->T3. T2->T3 on B? T3 writes B after T2 so T2->T3. Cycle? No. Actually this might be conflict serializable to T1, T2, T3. Let me try another:
T1: W(A)
T2: R(A), W(A)
T3: W(A)
This is not view serializable? I'm confused.

b) MVCC vs locking: MVCC uses versions, readers don't block writers. Locking blocks. Snapshot isolation: each transaction sees a consistent snapshot. Write skew: two transactions read overlapping data but write disjoint data based on stale reads.

Example: X=50, Y=50, constraint X+Y>0. T1: reads X=50, Y=50, writes X=-40. T2: reads X=50, Y=50, writes Y=-40. Both commit. X+Y=-80 violates constraint.
SSI: tracks dangerous structures like rw-antidependencies. Aborts one of the transactions to break the cycle.

Question 2
a) ARIES stands for Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics. Three phases:
1. Analysis: Scans log from last checkpoint. Rebuilds transaction table (active transactions with lastLSN) and dirty page table (dirty pages with recLSN). Determines winner and loser transactions.
2. Redo: Repeats history by applying all updates from the smallest recLSN in DPT. Uses pageLSN to avoid redundant redo.
3. Undo: Processes loser transactions in reverse order of their lastLSN. Writes CLRs for each undo operation.

DPT significance: tracks which pages are dirty and the earliest LSN that dirtied them. TT significance: tracks active transactions and their state.

Example operations:
L1: T1 updates P1 (before image, after image)
L2: T2 updates P2
L3: T1 commits
L4: T2 updates P1
Crash

At crash: T1 committed, T2 active. P1 has updates from T1 and T2. P2 has update from T2.
ARIES: Analysis finds T2 active, P1 dirty with recLSN=L1, P2 dirty with recLSN=L2. Redo applies L1, L2, L4. Undo undoes T2: undoes L4 writing CLR1, undoes L2 writing CLR2.

b) UNDO logging: writes before images to log before updating database. REDO logging: writes after images to log before updating. UNDO/REDO: writes both.

Steal policy: allows writing uncommitted data to disk. No-steal: does not allow. Force policy: ensures committed data is on disk. No-force: does not ensure.

UNDO logging requires no-steal (cannot write uncommitted data) but can have force or no-force? Actually UNDO logging requires force to ensure committed data is on disk before commit. REDO logging requires steal? No, REDO logging requires no-force and can have steal.

Physiological logging: combines physical logging (page-level) with logical logging (within page). Example: update page 5, offset 10, insert tuple (101, 'John', 50000).

Question 3
a) Clustered index: records physically stored in index order on data pages. Leaf pages contain actual records. Non-clustered index: leaf pages contain pointers (RIDs) to records in heap. 

Range queries: Clustered index is faster because records are on contiguous pages, enabling sequential I/O. Non-clustered index requires random I/O to fetch each record.

Single-record lookup: Non-clustered index may be slightly faster if index is smaller (fewer levels). Clustered index may require traversing deeper tree.

Employee table: Employee(ID, Name, Dept, Salary). 
Index-only scan: Non-clustered index on (Dept, Salary). Query: SELECT Dept, Salary FROM Employee WHERE Dept='Sales'. Index contains Dept and Salary, so no need to access heap. Reads only index pages (say 3 pages). Full table scan reads all data pages (say 1000 pages).
Clustered index scan: Clustered index on ID. Query: SELECT * FROM Employee WHERE ID BETWEEN 100 AND 200. Records 100-200 are on contiguous pages (say 5 pages). Sequential access is fast.

b) Extendible hashing: Uses a directory with 2^global_depth entries pointing to buckets. Each bucket has a local depth. When a bucket overflows, split it. If local depth == global depth, double directory.

Insert sequence with capacity 3: 1, 5, 7, 12, 2, 20
Initial: global_depth=1, directory=[0,1]. Bucket0: empty, Bucket1: empty.
Insert 1: hash(1)=01? Let's assume bucket 1: [1]
Insert 5: hash(5)=01? bucket 1: [1,5]
Insert 7: hash(7)=11? bucket 1? Actually this depends on hash function. I'll use simple mod 2.

This is getting complicated. I'll show partial evolution.

Linear hashing: splits buckets in round-robin order. Uses overflow chains. Directory grows linearly.

Average block access: Extendible hashing: 1-2. Linear hashing: 1-3 with overflow.

Question 4
a) External merge sort: Phase 1 sorts runs of size B pages. Phase 2+ merges runs. Cost = 2N * (number of passes).

Hybrid hash join: Partitions both relations into B-1 partitions. Build relation partition 0 is kept in memory. Other partitions are written to disk. Then joins each partition.

Grace hash join: Both relations are partitioned into B-1 partitions. Then each partition is joined in memory. Preferred over block nested loop join because it avoids repeated scans of the smaller relation.

5-pass merge sort: N=5000, B=50. Pass 0: 5000/50=100 runs. Merge 100 runs with 49 buffers: ceil(log_49(100)) = ceil(1.18) = 2 passes. Total passes = 3. Cost = 2*5000*3 = 30000 I/O.

Hybrid hash join: 25% of memory reserved = 12.5 buffers. Build relation partition 0 = 12.5 pages (assuming 1 page per buffer). Cost = 3*5000 - 2*12.5 = 14975 I/O.

b) Volcano model: uses iterator interface, each operator produces one tuple at a time. Function call per tuple causes overhead.

Vectorized execution: processes batches of tuples (e.g., 1000 tuples) at once. Reduces function call overhead, enables SIMD.

MPP model: shared-nothing architecture, data partitioned across nodes, each node executes part of query in parallel. Results are combined.

Columnar storage: stores data column by column. Better compression because same type data. Predicate pushdown can skip entire columns.

JIT compilation: converts query plan into machine code. Reduces interpretation overhead. For star schema query with multiple joins, JIT can compile join loops for specific data types, reducing per-row overhead significantly.
